title: Book 1, Chapter 5 — Second Congress at Lacedaemon—Preparations for War and Diplomatic Skirmishes—Cylon—Pausanias—Themistocles
paragraphs: After this, though not many years later, we at last come to what has already been described—the affairs of Corcyra and Potidæa, and the events that served as the pretext for the present war. All these actions of the Hellenes against each other and against the barbarian took place in the fifty-year interval between the retreat of Xerxes and the beginning of the present war. During this interval the Athenians succeeded in placing their empire on a firmer footing and raised their own home power to a very great height. The Lacedaemonians, fully aware of it, opposed it only briefly, but stayed inactive most of the time, being from of old slow to go to war except under pressure of necessity, and at this moment hampered by wars at home. Eventually the growth of Athenian power could no longer be ignored, and their own confederacy became the object of its encroachments. Then they felt they could endure it no longer; the time had come to throw themselves heart and soul against the hostile power and break it, if they could, by starting the present war. Although the Lacedaemonians had already decided that the treaty was broken and the Athenians were guilty, they still sent to Delphi and asked the god whether it would go well with them if they went to war; and, as the story goes, they received the answer that if they put their whole strength into the war, victory would be theirs, and the promise that he himself would be with them, whether invoked or not. Still they wanted to summon their allies again and take a vote on whether to make war. After the ambassadors from the confederates had arrived and a congress had been convened, they all spoke their minds, most of them denouncing the Athenians and demanding that the war begin. The Corinthians in particular. They had already, on their own account, been canvassing the cities one by one to induce them to vote for war, fearing it might come too late to save Potidæa. They were present on this occasion as well, came forward last, and made the following speech:

“Fellow allies, we can no longer accuse the Lacedaemonians of having failed in their duty: they have not only voted for war themselves, but have assembled us here for that purpose. We say their duty, because supremacy has its duties. Beyond fairly administering private interests, leaders are required to show special care for the common welfare, in return for the special honours accorded them by everyone in other ways. As for ourselves, all who have already had dealings with the Athenians need no warning to be on guard against them. The states more inland, off the main lines of communication, should understand that if they fail to support the coast powers, the result will be to hurt the transit of their produce for export and the receipt in exchange of their imports from the sea. They must not weigh what is now said as if it had nothing to do with them. They should expect that the sacrifice of the powers on the coast will one day be followed by the extension of the danger to the interior, and recognise that their own interests are deeply involved in this discussion. For these reasons they should not hesitate to exchange peace for war. Wise men remain quiet so long as they are not injured; brave men abandon peace for war when they are injured, returning to an understanding when a favourable opportunity arises. They are neither intoxicated by their success in war nor disposed to put up with an injury for the sake of the delightful tranquillity of peace. To falter for the sake of such delights is, if you remain inactive, the quickest way to lose the very repose you cling to; while to form extravagant ambitions out of success in war is to forget how hollow the confidence is that elates you. For if many ill-conceived plans have succeeded thanks to the still greater stupidity of an opponent, many more, apparently well-laid, have ended in disgrace. The confidence with which we form our schemes is never fully justified in carrying them out; speculation is safe, but when it comes to action, fear causes failure.

“To apply these rules to ourselves: if we are now kindling war, it is under the pressure of injury, with adequate grounds of complaint; and once we have punished the Athenians, we will desist in good time. We have many reasons to expect success—first, superiority in numbers and in military experience; and second, our general and unvarying obedience in carrying out orders. The naval strength they possess we shall raise from our existing resources and from the funds at Olympia and Delphi. A loan from these will let us seduce their foreign sailors by offering higher pay. For the power of Athens is more mercenary than national; ours will not be exposed to the same risk, since its strength lies more in men than in money. A single defeat at sea is in all likelihood their ruin: should they hold out, in that case there will be all the more time for us to train ourselves in naval matters; and once we have reached equality in skill, we hardly need ask whether we shall surpass them in courage. The advantages we have by nature they cannot acquire by training; while their superiority in skill must be removed by our practice. The money required for these objects shall be supplied by our contributions: nothing could be more monstrous than the suggestion that, while their allies never tire of contributing for their own enslavement, we should refuse to spend on vengeance and self-preservation the treasure which by such refusal we shall forfeit to Athenian rapacity and see used for our own ruin.

“We also have other ways of carrying on the war, such as inciting their allies to revolt—the surest way to deprive Athens of the revenues that are the source of her strength—and establishing fortified positions in their country, along with various operations that cannot be foreseen at present. War, more than anything, proceeds least by definite rules, and draws chiefly on its own resources to meet emergencies; in such cases the side that faces the struggle and keeps its temper best meets with most security, and the side that loses its temper meets with corresponding disaster. Let us also reflect that if it were merely a matter of disputes over territory between rival neighbours, it might be borne; but here we have an enemy in Athens that is a match for our whole coalition, and more than a match for any of its members. So unless, as a body and as individual peoples and individual cities, we make a unanimous stand against her, she will easily conquer us, divided and in detail. That conquest, terrible as it may sound, would mean nothing less than slavery, plain and simple—a word the Peloponnese cannot even hear whispered without disgrace, or watch so many states abused by one without disgrace. The opinion would be either that we deserved it, or that we put up with it from cowardice and were proving degenerate sons by failing to secure even the freedom our fathers gave to Hellas, and by allowing the establishment of a tyrant state in Hellas, even though within our own individual states we think it our duty to put down sole rulers. We do not see how this conduct can be cleared of three of the gravest failings—want of sense, want of courage, and want of vigilance. We do not suppose that you have taken refuge in that contempt for an enemy which has proved fatal in so many cases—a feeling which, from the numbers it has ruined, has come to be called not contemptuous but contemptible.

“There is no advantage in reflections on the past beyond what serves the present. For the future we must provide by holding what we have and redoubling our efforts. It is hereditary to us to win virtue as the fruit of labour, and you must not change the habit, even if you have a slight advantage in wealth and resources. It is not right that what was won in want should be lost in plenty. We must boldly advance to war for many reasons: the god has commanded it and promised to be with us, and the rest of Hellas will all join in the struggle, partly from fear, partly from interest. You will not be the first to break a treaty which the god, by counselling us to go to war, judges already broken; rather you will be supporting a treaty that has been outraged. Treaties are broken not by resistance but by aggression.

“Your position, then, from any angle you view it, will amply justify you in going to war; and we recommend this step in the interests of all, remembering that identity of interest is the surest of bonds, whether between states or individuals. Do not delay to assist Potidæa, a Dorian city besieged by Ionians, which is a complete reversal of the natural order, nor to assert the freedom of the rest. We can wait no longer when waiting can only mean immediate disaster for some of us, and—if it becomes known that we have conferred but do not dare to protect ourselves—the same disaster in the near future for the rest. Do not delay, fellow allies, but, convinced of the necessity of the crisis and the wisdom of this counsel, vote for war—undeterred by its immediate terrors and looking beyond to the lasting peace that will succeed it. Out of war peace gains fresh stability, but to refuse to abandon repose for war is no surer way of avoiding danger. We must believe that the tyrant city established in Hellas has been established against all alike, with a programme of universal empire, part of it already achieved, the rest in contemplation. Let us then attack it, reduce it, and win future security for ourselves and freedom for the Hellenes who are now enslaved.”

Such were the words of the Corinthians. Having now heard everyone, the Lacedaemonians took the vote of all the allied states present, in turn, great and small alike; and the majority voted for war. With this decided, it was still impossible to begin at once, since they were not prepared. It was resolved that each state should procure the necessary means and that there should be no delay. Yet, despite the time taken up by the necessary arrangements, less than a year passed before Attica was invaded and the war openly begun.

This interval was spent sending embassies to Athens with complaints, in order to obtain as good a pretext for war as possible if she paid no attention to them. The first Lacedaemonian embassy ordered the Athenians to drive out the curse of the goddess. Its history is as follows. In former generations there was an Athenian named Cylon, an Olympic victor, of good birth and powerful position, who had married a daughter of Theagenes, a Megarian, then tyrant of Megara. This Cylon was inquiring at Delphi when the god told him to seize the Acropolis of Athens at the grand festival of Zeus. Accordingly, getting a force from Theagenes and persuading his friends to join him, when the Olympic festival in the Peloponnese came around, he seized the Acropolis with the intention of making himself tyrant. He thought this was the grand festival of Zeus and an occasion fitting for an Olympic victor. Whether the festival meant was in Attica or elsewhere was a question he never thought about, and the oracle did not offer to settle it. The Athenians too have a festival called the grand festival of Zeus Meilichios, the Gracious—the Diasia. It is celebrated outside the city, where the whole people sacrifice not real victims but a number of bloodless offerings peculiar to the country. Convinced he had picked the right time, he made the attempt. As soon as the Athenians realised what was happening, they flocked in from the country, every man of them, and sat down to besiege the citadel. As time wore on, weary of the labour of blockade, most of them went home, leaving responsibility for the watch to the nine archons, with full powers to settle everything as they saw fit. It must be remembered that at that time most political functions were carried out by the nine archons. Meanwhile Cylon and his besieged companions were in distress for want of food and water. Cylon and his brother managed to escape; but the rest, hard pressed and some even dying of hunger, sat as suppliants at the altar in the Acropolis. The Athenians on guard duty, when they saw them at the point of death in the temple, raised them up on the understanding that no harm would be done to them, led them out, and killed them. Some who took refuge as they passed by at the altars of the awful goddesses were dispatched on the spot. From this deed the men who killed them were called accursed and guilty against the goddess—they and their descendants. These cursed ones were driven out by the Athenians, then driven out again by Cleomenes of Lacedaemon and an Athenian faction; the living were expelled and the bones of the dead taken up; thus they were cast out. Even so they came back later, and their descendants are still in the city.

This, then, was the curse the Lacedaemonians ordered them to drive out. They were primarily motivated, as they pretended, by concern for the honour of the gods. But they also knew that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was connected with the curse on his mother’s side, and they thought his banishment would substantially advance their designs on Athens. Not that they really expected to succeed; rather they meant to create prejudice against him in the eyes of his countrymen, suggesting that the war would be partly caused by his bad luck. For he was the most powerful man of his time and the leading Athenian statesman, and he opposed the Lacedaemonians on every issue, refused all concessions, and constantly urged the Athenians on toward war.

The Athenians retorted by ordering the Lacedaemonians to drive out the curse of Taenarus. The Lacedaemonians had once raised some Helot suppliants from the temple of Poseidon at Taenarus, led them away, and killed them; for which they believe the great earthquake at Sparta was retribution. The Athenians also ordered them to drive out the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House, the history of which is as follows. After Pausanias the Lacedaemonian had been recalled by the Spartans from his command in the Hellespont (this was his first recall), and had been tried by them and acquitted, he was not sent out again in any official capacity. He took a galley of Hermione on his own responsibility, without Lacedaemonian authority, and arrived as a private person in the Hellespont. He came ostensibly for the Hellenic war, but really to pursue his intrigues with the King, which he had begun before his recall, ambitious to rule over Hellas. The circumstance that first allowed him to put the King in his debt and to begin the whole design was this. Some of the King’s connections and kinsmen had been captured at Byzantium when the city was taken from the Medes, when Pausanias was first there after the return from Cyprus. He sent these prisoners off to the King without the knowledge of the rest of the allies, with the cover story that they had escaped. He arranged this with the help of Gongylus, an Eretrian, whom he had put in charge of Byzantium and the prisoners. He also gave Gongylus a letter for the King, the contents of which—as was later discovered—were as follows: “Pausanias, the general of Sparta, eager to do you a favour, sends you these prisoners of war. I propose also, with your approval, to marry your daughter and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you. I believe I am able to do this, with your cooperation. So if any of this pleases you, send a trusty man to the sea through whom we may carry on our future correspondence.”

That was all that was revealed in the writing, and Xerxes was pleased with the letter. He sent off Artabazus, son of Pharnaces, to the sea with orders to replace Megabates, the previous governor of the satrapy of Daskylion, and to send across as quickly as possible a letter—entrusted to him—for Pausanias at Byzantium; to show him the royal seal; and to carry out any commission Pausanias might give him on the King’s business with all care and fidelity. Artabazus, on arriving, carried out the King’s orders and sent over the letter, which contained this answer: “Thus says King Xerxes to Pausanias. For the men whom you have saved for me from across the sea from Byzantium, an obligation is laid up for you in our house, recorded forever; and with your proposals I am well pleased. Let neither night nor day stop you from diligently performing any of your promises to me. Let neither cost in gold nor in silver hold them back, nor any number of troops, wherever their presence is needed; but with Artabazus, an honourable man whom I send you, boldly advance my objects and yours, in whatever way most serves the honour and interest of us both.”

Already held in high honour among the Hellenes as the hero of Plataea, Pausanias, after receiving this letter, became prouder than ever, and could no longer live in the usual style. He went out of Byzantium in Median dress, was attended on his march through Thrace by a bodyguard of Medes and Egyptians, kept a Persian table, and was quite unable to contain his intentions; he betrayed in trifles what his ambition meant one day to enact on a grander scale. He also made himself difficult to approach, and showed so violent a temper to everyone, without exception, that no one could come near him. This indeed was the principal reason the confederacy went over to the Athenians.

This conduct, when it came to the ears of the Lacedaemonians, occasioned his first recall. After his second voyage out in the Hermione ship, without their orders, he gave further proofs of similar behaviour. Besieged and expelled from Byzantium by the Athenians, he did not return to Sparta. News came that he had settled at Colonae in the Troad and was intriguing with the barbarians, and that his stay there was for no good purpose. The ephors, no longer hesitating, sent him a herald and a scytale with orders to accompany the herald or be declared a public enemy. Anxious above all to avoid suspicion, and confident he could quash the charge with money, he returned a second time to Sparta. At first thrown into prison by the ephors—whose powers allow them to do this even to the King—he soon compromised the matter, was released, and offered himself for trial to anyone who wished to bring an inquiry against him.

The Spartans had no tangible proof against him—neither his enemies nor the nation at large had any of that indisputable kind required for the punishment of a member of the royal family who was at that moment in high office. He was regent for his first cousin King Pleistarchus, son of Leonidas, who was still a minor. But by his contempt for the laws and his imitation of the barbarians, he gave grounds for much suspicion that he was discontented with the established order. All the occasions on which he had departed in any way from the regular customs were reviewed, and it was remembered that he had taken it upon himself to have inscribed on the tripod at Delphi—dedicated by the Hellenes as the first-fruits of the spoils of the Medes—the following couplet:
The Mede defeated, great Pausanias raised This monument, that Phœbus might be praised.

At the time the Lacedaemonians had erased the couplet at once and inscribed instead the names of the cities that had aided in the overthrow of the barbarian and dedicated the offering. Pausanias was considered to have been guilty of a grave offence here—one which, interpreted in the light of the attitude he had since taken, gained a new significance and seemed perfectly in keeping with his current schemes. They were also informed that he was even intriguing with the Helots; and so it was, for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would join him in revolt and help him carry out his plans to the end. Even now, mistrusting the evidence even of the Helots themselves, the ephors would not consent to take any decisive step against him, in line with their regular custom toward fellow Spartans—to be slow to take any irrevocable decision in the case of a Spartan citizen without indisputable proof. At last, it is said, the man who was to carry the latest letter to Artabazus for the King, an Argilian and once Pausanias’s favourite and most trusted servant, turned informer. Alarmed by the thought that none of the previous messengers had ever returned, he had counterfeited the seal so that, if he were mistaken in his suspicions, or if Pausanias asked to make some change, he would not be found out. He undid the letter and found the postscript he had suspected—an order to put him to death.

On being shown the letter, the ephors now felt more certain. Still they wanted to hear Pausanias commit himself with their own ears. So the man went, by appointment, to Taenarus as a suppliant, and there built himself a hut divided in two by a partition; behind it he hid some of the ephors and let them hear the whole matter plainly. Pausanias came to him and asked the reason for his suppliant position; the man reproached him with the order he had written about him, and one by one declared all the rest of the circumstances—how, although Pausanias had never yet brought him into any danger when he was employed as agent between him and the King, he was now to be rewarded with death like the rest of his servants. Admitting all this and telling him not to be angry about it, Pausanias gave him his pledge to raise him up from the temple, and begged him to set off as quickly as possible and not to delay the business in hand.

The ephors listened carefully and then left, taking no action for the moment. Now that they had certainty at last, they were preparing to arrest him in the city. It is reported that, just as he was about to be arrested in the street, he saw from the face of one of the ephors what he was coming for; another, too, made him a secret signal, betraying it out of kindness. Setting off at a run for the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House, the precinct of which was nearby, he managed to take sanctuary before they could seize him, and entered a small chamber that formed part of the temple, to keep out of the weather, where he lay still. The ephors, having lost ground in the pursuit, afterwards took the roof off the chamber and, having made sure he was inside, shut him in, barricaded the doors, and stayed in front of the place, reducing him by starvation. When they found he was on the point of dying, just as he was, in the chamber, they brought him out of the temple while the breath was still in him, and as soon as he was outside he died. They were going to throw him into the Kaiadas, where they cast criminals, but in the end they decided to bury him somewhere nearby. Later the god at Delphi ordered the Lacedaemonians to move the tomb to the place of his death—where he now lies in the consecrated ground, as an inscription on a monument declares—and, since what had been done was a curse on them, to give back two bodies instead of one to the goddess of the Brazen House. So they had two bronze statues made and dedicated them as a substitute for Pausanias. The Athenians retorted by telling the Lacedaemonians to drive out what the god himself had pronounced a curse.

To return to the Medism of Pausanias. Material was found in the course of the inquiry that implicated Themistocles. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent envoys to the Athenians, demanding that he be punished as Pausanias had been. The Athenians agreed. As it happened, however, he had been ostracised, and, while living at Argos, was in the habit of visiting other parts of the Peloponnese. So the Athenians sent agents along with the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join the pursuit, with instructions to take him wherever they found him. But Themistocles got wind of their intentions and fled from the Peloponnese to Corcyra, which was under obligations to him. The Corcyraeans claimed they could not risk sheltering him at the cost of offending Athens and Lacedaemon, and they conveyed him over to the continent opposite. Pursued by officers who hung on every report of his movements, at a loss where to turn, he was forced to stop at the house of Admetus, the Molossian king, though they were not on friendly terms. Admetus happened not to be at home, but his wife, to whom he made himself a suppliant, instructed him to take their child in his arms and sit down by the hearth. Soon afterwards Admetus came in, and Themistocles told him who he was and begged him not to take revenge on a Themistocles in exile for any opposition his requests might have met from Themistocles at Athens. He was now far too low for revenge; retaliation was honourable only between equals. Besides, his opposition to the king had affected only the success of a request, not the safety of his person; if the king were to hand him over to the pursuers he had mentioned, and to the fate they intended for him, he would simply be consigning him to certain death.

The King listened to him and raised him up along with his son, who was sitting in his arms in the most effective form of supplication. When the Lacedaemonians arrived not long afterwards, he refused to give him up, no matter what they said, but sent him by land to the other sea, to Pydna in Alexander’s dominions, since Themistocles wished to go to the Persian king. There he met a merchantman about to sail for Ionia. He boarded her and was carried by a storm to the Athenian squadron blockading Naxos. In his alarm—he was luckily unknown to the people on board—he told the master who he was and what he was fleeing, and warned that if the master refused to save him he would say he was being carried for a bribe. Their safety, he pointed out, lay in letting no one leave the ship until a favourable time for sailing arose. If the master complied with his wishes, he promised him a proper reward. The master did as he asked, and after lying to for a day and a night out of reach of the squadron, finally arrived at Ephesus.

After rewarding him with a gift of money, as soon as he received some from his friends at Athens and from his secret hoards at Argos, Themistocles set off inland with one of the coastal Persians, and sent a letter to King Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, who had just come to the throne. Its contents were as follows: “I, Themistocles, have come to you—I who did your house more harm than any of the Hellenes, when I was forced to defend myself against your father’s invasion—harm, however, far surpassed by the good I did him during his retreat, which carried no danger for me but much for him. For the past, you owe me a good turn”—here he mentioned the warning sent to Xerxes from Salamis to retreat, as well as his finding the bridges unbroken, which he falsely claimed was due to him—“for the present, able to do you great service, I am here, pursued by the Hellenes for my friendship for you. I ask, however, for a year’s grace, after which I shall be able to declare in person the objects of my coming.”

It is said the King approved his intention and told him to do as he proposed. He spent the interval making what progress he could in the study of the Persian tongue and the customs of the country. Arriving at court at the end of the year, he attained a higher consideration there than any Hellene before or since—partly because of his splendid background, partly because of the hopes he held out of subjecting Hellas to the King, but principally because of the proof his capacity gave every day. For Themistocles was a man who showed the most unmistakable signs of genius; in this he has a claim on our admiration that is quite extraordinary and unparalleled. By his own native ability, neither shaped nor supplemented by study, he was at once the best judge in those sudden crises that admit of little or no deliberation, and the best prophet of the future, even to its most distant possibilities. An able theoretical expositor of all that came within his practical experience, he was not without the power of passing an adequate judgment on matters in which he had no experience. He could also discern with rare skill the good and evil hidden in the unseen future. In short, whether we consider the extent of his natural powers or the slightness of his application, this extraordinary man must be granted to have surpassed all others in the faculty of intuitively meeting an emergency. Disease was the real cause of his death, though there is a story that he ended his life by poison on finding himself unable to fulfil his promises to the king. However that may be, there is a monument to him in the marketplace of Asiatic Magnesia. He was governor of the district, the King having given him Magnesia, which brought in fifty talents a year, for bread; Lampsacus, considered the richest wine country, for wine; and Myos for other provisions. His bones, it is said, were brought home by his relatives in accordance with his wishes and buried in Attic soil. This was done without the knowledge of the Athenians, since it is against the law to bury in Attica an outlaw for treason. So ends the history of Pausanias and Themistocles—the Lacedaemonian and the Athenian—the most famous men of their time in Hellas.

To return to the Lacedaemonians. The history of their first embassy, the demands it conveyed, and the reply it provoked, concerning the expulsion of the accursed persons, has already been told. It was followed by a second embassy, which ordered Athens to raise the siege of Potidæa and to respect the independence of Aegina. Above all, it gave her clearly to understand that war could be averted by revoking the Megara decree, which excluded the Megarians from Athenian harbours and from the market of Athens. But Athens was not inclined either to revoke the decree or to consider their other proposals. She accused the Megarians of pushing their cultivation onto the consecrated ground and the unenclosed land on the border, and of harbouring her runaway slaves. At last an embassy arrived with the Lacedaemonian ultimatum. The ambassadors were Ramphias, Melesippus, and Agesander. Not a word was said on any of the old subjects; there was simply this: “Lacedaemon wishes the peace to continue, and there is no reason it should not, if you would leave the Hellenes independent.” On this, the Athenians held an assembly and laid the matter before them. It was resolved to deliberate once for all on all their demands and to give them an answer. Many speakers came forward and supported one side or the other, urging either the necessity of war, or the revocation of the decree and the folly of letting it stand in the way of peace. Among them came forward Pericles, son of Xanthippus, the foremost man of his time at Athens, ablest alike in counsel and in action, and gave the following advice:

“There is one principle, Athenians, which I hold to through everything: the principle of no concession to the Peloponnesians. I know that the spirit which inspires men while they are being persuaded to make war is not always retained in action; that as circumstances change, resolutions change. Yet I see that now, as before, almost literally the same counsel is being asked of me. I appeal to those of you who are letting yourselves be persuaded to support the national resolves even in the case of reverses, or to forfeit all credit for their wisdom in the event of success. For sometimes the course of events is as arbitrary as the plans of men; this is why we usually blame chance for whatever does not happen as we expected. It was clear before that Lacedaemon was scheming against us; it is even clearer now. The treaty provides that we shall mutually submit our differences to legal settlement, and that we shall meanwhile each keep what we have. Yet the Lacedaemonians have never made us such an offer, nor would they accept one from us; on the contrary, they wish complaints to be settled by war instead of by negotiation, and now we find them here dropping the tone of expostulation and adopting that of command. They order us to raise the siege of Potidæa, to let Aegina be independent, to revoke the Megara decree—and they conclude with an ultimatum warning us to leave the Hellenes independent. I hope none of you will think we shall be going to war for a trifle if we refuse to revoke the Megara decree, which heads their list of complaints, and the revocation of which is supposed to save us from war. Let no feeling of self-reproach linger in your minds, as if you were going to war for a slight cause. This trifle contains the whole seal and trial of your resolve. If you give way, you will at once be faced with some greater demand, having shown yourselves frightened into obedience the first time; while a firm refusal will make them clearly understand that they must treat you more as equals. Make your decision now, then—either to submit before you are harmed, or, if we are to go to war (as I for one think we should), to do so without caring whether the ostensible cause is great or small, resolved against making concessions or holding our possessions on a precarious tenure. For all claims from an equal, urged on a neighbour as commands before any attempt at legal settlement, whether they be great or small, have only one meaning, and that is slavery.

“As to the war and the resources of the two sides, a detailed comparison will not show you any inferiority on Athens’s side. Personally engaged in cultivating their land, without funds private or public, the Peloponnesians are also without experience of long wars across the sea, since the strict limit poverty places on them confines their attacks to each other. Powers of this description are quite incapable of often manning a fleet or often sending out an army: they cannot afford the absence from their homes or the expenditure from their own funds, and besides they have no command of the sea. Capital, remember, sustains a war more than forced contributions. Farmers are a class of men always more ready to serve in person than in purse. Confident that their persons will survive the dangers, they are by no means so sure their funds will not run out prematurely, especially if the war drags on longer than they expect, which is very likely. In a single battle the Peloponnesians and their allies may be able to defy all Hellas; but they are unable to wage war against a power of a different character from their own, because they lack the single council-chamber needed for prompt and vigorous action. Instead they have a diet composed of various peoples, in which every state has an equal vote and each pushes its own ends—a state of affairs that generally results in no action at all. Some are mainly interested in revenging themselves on a particular enemy, others in saving their own pockets. Slow in assembling, they devote a very small fraction of their time to considering any public matter, and most of it to pursuing their own. Meanwhile each fancies that no harm will come of his neglect, that it is somebody else’s business to look after this or that for him; and so, as the same notion is held by everyone separately, the common cause imperceptibly decays.

“But the principal point is the difficulty they will face from lack of money. The slowness with which it comes in will cause delay; and the opportunities of war wait for no one. Nor need we be alarmed at the possibility of their raising fortifications in Attica, or at their navy. It would be hard for any system of fortifications to establish a rival city even in time of peace, much less in an enemy’s country, with Athens just as well fortified against it as it against Athens. A mere outpost might be able to do some harm to the country by raids and by providing facilities for desertion, but it can never prevent us from sailing into their country and raising fortifications there, and making reprisals with our powerful fleet. For our naval skill is of more use to us for service on land than their military skill for service at sea. They will not find familiarity with the sea easy to acquire. If you, who have been practising at it ever since the Median invasion, have not yet brought it to perfection, what chance is there of any considerable result from an agricultural, unseafaring population, who will besides be prevented from practising by the constant presence of strong observation squadrons from Athens? With a small squadron they might risk an engagement, encouraging their ignorance with numbers; but the restraint of a strong force will keep them from moving, and through lack of practice they will grow more clumsy, and so more timid. It must be remembered that seamanship, like anything else, is a matter of skill, and will not allow itself to be taken up occasionally as a pursuit for leisure time. On the contrary, it is so demanding that it leaves leisure for nothing else.

“Even if they were to touch the funds at Olympia or Delphi, and try to seduce our foreign sailors with the lure of higher pay, that would be a serious danger only if we could not still match them by manning our ships with our own citizens and the resident aliens among us. As it is, we can always match them by this means; and, best of all, we have a larger and higher class of native coxswains and sailors among our own citizens than all the rest of Hellas put together. To say nothing of the danger of such a step, none of our foreign sailors would consent to become an outlaw from his country and take service with the Peloponnesians and their hopes for the sake of a few days’ high pay.

“This, I think, is a fair enough account of the position of the Peloponnesians; the position of Athens is free from the defects I have criticised in them and has other advantages of its own which they cannot equal. If they march against our country, we will sail against theirs, and it will then turn out that the desolation of all of Attica is not the same thing as the desolation of even a fraction of the Peloponnese; for they will not be able to make up the deficiency except by a battle, while we have plenty of land both on the islands and on the mainland. The rule of the sea is indeed a great matter. Consider for a moment. Suppose we were islanders—can you imagine a more impregnable position? Well, this should, as far as possible, be our conception of our position from now on. Dismissing all thought of our land and houses, we must vigilantly guard the sea and the city. No irritation we may feel about the former must provoke us into a battle with the numerical superiority of the Peloponnesians. A victory would only be followed by another battle against the same superiority; a reverse would mean the loss of our allies, the source of our strength, who will not stay quiet a day longer than we are unable to march against them. We must mourn not the loss of houses and land but the loss of men’s lives; for houses and land do not gain us men, but men gain us houses and land. And if I had thought I could persuade you, I would have told you to go out and lay them waste with your own hands, and show the Peloponnesians that this, at least, will not make you submit.

“I have many other reasons to hope for a favourable outcome, if you will agree not to combine schemes of fresh conquest with the conduct of the war, and will refrain from wilfully exposing yourselves to other dangers. I am more afraid of our own blunders than of the enemy’s designs. But these matters shall be explained in another speech, as events require. For the present, dismiss these men with this answer: we will allow Megara the use of our market and harbours when the Lacedaemonians suspend their alien acts in our favour and our allies’, there being nothing in the treaty to prevent either; we will leave the cities independent, if they were independent when we made the treaty, and when the Lacedaemonians grant their cities an independence not consisting of subservience to Lacedaemonian interests but such as each may severally desire; we are willing to give the legal satisfaction our agreements provide for, and we shall not commence hostilities, but shall resist those who do. This is an answer that suits both the rights and the dignity of Athens. It must be thoroughly understood that war is a necessity; and that the more readily we accept it, the less ardent our opponents will be; and that out of the greatest dangers communities and individuals acquire the greatest glory. Did not our fathers resist the Medes not only with resources far different from ours, but even when those resources had been abandoned? More by wisdom than by fortune, more by daring than by strength, did they not beat off the barbarian and bring our affairs to their present height? We must not fall behind them, but must resist our enemies in any way and in every way, and try to hand on our power to our descendants unimpaired.”

Such were the words of Pericles. The Athenians, persuaded of the wisdom of his advice, voted as he wished, and answered the Lacedaemonians as he recommended, both on the separate points and in general: they would do nothing under dictation, but were ready to have the complaints settled in a fair and impartial manner by the legal method which the terms of the truce prescribed. So the envoys went home and did not return again.

These were the charges and disputes existing between the rival powers before the war, arising immediately out of the affair at Epidamnus and Corcyra. Still, dealings continued in spite of them, with mutual communication. It was carried on without heralds, but not without suspicion, since events were occurring which amounted to a breach of the treaty and grounds for war.
